Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines

crazy adjective

mad

also mad (insane), insane, madness, go crazy, you’re crazy, nuts, be crazy about, are you quite all there?, are you out of your mind?, drive someone mad, go mad, he’s out of his mind, he’s nuts, out of one’s mind, I was out of my mind when, you’re nuts, demented, deranged, insanity, nutty, he is a nut

classical

Cic. Ac. 2.52 (Lewis & Short)
Hor. S. 2.6.29: quid tibi vīs, īnsāne?
Traupman 154
Traupman 333

īnsānus, īnsāna, īnsānum

Declension on Wiktionary

mad, crazy

Unsound in mind, and in talk of anyone behaving wildly: “you madman!”. The verb īnsāniō, īnsānīre is to be mad, to act crazily; īnsānia is madness.

Other words

  • dēmēns, dēmentis — out of one’s mind; senseless

    also used · classical · Cic. N.D. 1.94: dēsipere, dēlīrāre, dēmentēs esse (Lewis & Short); Traupman 151; Traupman 302 · Declension on Wiktionary

    Very common in Cicero, of a mind gone or a senseless act.

  • dēlīrus, dēlīra, dēlīrum — silly, doting, crazy

    also used · classical · Cic. de Or. 2.75: senex (Lewis & Short); Traupman 150, 298, 151 · Declension on Wiktionary

    From dē līrā, out of the furrow; of an old man in his dotage, or anyone talking nonsense. The verb is dēlīrō.

  • cerrītus, cerrīta, cerrītum — cracked, crazy

    also used · classical · Plaut. Amph. 2.2.144 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 298 · Declension on Wiktionary

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut.; Hor. S. 2.3.278)

    Of a crazed brain. To be crazy about someone is dēperīre (Traupman 96: eam dēperit).

  • Satin' sānus es? — are you quite all there? are you mad?

    also used · classical · Ter. Ad. 937; Traupman 92

    Satin' is satisne clipped: “are you sane enough?”

  • dēmentem facere (aliquem) — drive someone mad

    also used · modern · Traupman 97; Traupman 307

    Traupman’s phrase, of classical words; not found as a phrase in Lewis & Short or the loci.

  • mente aliēnārī — go mad, be out of one’s mind

    passive of aliēnāre, with the ablative mente · also used · classical · Plin. NH 28.93: aliēnārī mente, to be insane (Lewis & Short s.v. aliēnō); Traupman 103: to go mad, mente aliēnārī

    Literally “to be estranged from one’s mind”. Lewis & Short: the sense “drive mad” is not found before the Augustan age; the participle is the usual form, mente aliēnātus, out of his mind.

  • aliēnātus ā sē — out of his mind

    also used · modern · Traupman 103: he’s out of his mind, aliēnātus est ā sē; Traupman 104: he’s nuts, aliēnātus est ā sē

    Traupman’s phrase. Lewis & Short has aliēnātus mente and aliēnātus sēnsibus (Liv. 25.39) for madness, but not ā sē, which classically would mean “estranged from himself”; mente aliēnātus est says the same thing in attested words.

  • dēlīrō, dēlīrāre — be crazy, talk nonsense; you’re nuts!

    verb, first conjugation, intransitive · also used · classical · Cic. N. D. 1.94: dēsipere, dēlīrāre, dēmentēs esse (Lewis & Short); Traupman 104: you’re nuts, dēlīrās · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    Literally “to go out of the furrow” (līra). To someone talking nonsense: Dēlīrās!.

  • commōtus, commōta, commōtum — disturbed, deranged

    also used · classical · Traupman 151; Hor. S. 2.3.209: commōtus habēbitur (Lewis & Short s.v. commoveō, “frantic, crazed”); Traupman 303 · Declension on Wiktionary

    The participle of commovēre, “stirred up”, said of a disturbed mind.

  • īnsānitās, īnsānitātis f. — unsoundness of mind

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Tusc. 3.8 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 154; Traupman 333 · Declension on Wiktionary

    Cicero uses it to explain the ordinary word for madness, īnsānia.

  • mente captus, mente capta — out of one’s mind (of a person)

    also used · classical · Cic. Cat. 3: quis potest esse tam mente captus, quī neget? (Lewis & Short s.v. quī, cited as Cat. 3, 9); Traupman 303

  • baceolus, baceola, baceolum — nutty, daft

    also used · classical · Suet. Aug. 87: Augustus’ word for stultus (Lewis & Short); Traupman 352 · Declension on Wiktionary

    (vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī: Augustus apud Suet.)

Examples

  • quid tibi vīs, īnsāne?

    what do you want, you madman?Hor. S. 2.6.29

  • īnsānīre libet quoniam tibi

    since you want to be crazyVerg. Ecl. 3.36

  • quidquid dēlīrant rēgēs, plectuntur Achīvī

    whatever madness the kings commit, it is the Greeks who payHor. Ep. 1.2.14

  • Age, dā veniam fīliō. — Satin' sānus es?

    Come on, forgive the boy. — Are you quite all there?Ter. Ad. 937

  • Dēsipiēbam mentis cum illa scrīpta mittēbam tibi.

    I was out of my mind when I sent you that letter.Plaut. Epid. 1.2.35 (Lewis & Short s.v. dēsipiō)

  • Morbōsus est in lūdōs.

    He’s crazy about sports.Traupman 298

  • Aliēnātus est ā sē.

    He’s out of his mind.Traupman 346

  • Nūga iste est.

    He is a nut.Traupman 352

  • amīcōs habet merās nūgās

    he has friends who are mere triflersCic. Att. 6.3.5 (Lewis & Short s.v. nūgae)

  • Dēlīrās.

    You’re nuts.Traupman 352

See also angry, mental.
